transcript:
Header: Date/Time: 2027-04-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jasper Liu (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (CTO - Halcyon), Ravi Singh (Head of Cloud Ops), Sofia Morales (Security Architect)
Links referenced: Private Networking guide (link), SOC2 + compliance pack (link), Benchmark spreadsheet (link)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I’m Maya, AE for Redwood inference, and Jasper is our SE. Can each of you intro?
[00:12] Elena: Hi, I’m Elena, CTO at Halcyon, we run a clinical summarization pipeline and evals, looking to POC private deployment for PHI use.
[00:18] Ravi: Ravi here, we own cloud infra, VPCs in us-east-1 and us-west-2, curious about peering vs PrivateLink and egress restrictions.
[00:25] Sofia: Hi, Sofia - security, SOC2 background, will need audit logs, KMS integration, and hard data residency guarantees.
[00:32] Jasper: Thanks, quick agenda: understand workload (sizes/throughput), agree success criteria, pick networking approach, confirm benchmarks and timeline.

[00:45] Maya: To set expectations, our Private networking options are basically: VPC peering (direct peering into Redwood-managed VPC), or AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints. Peering is simpler for high-throughput but requires cross-account routing. PrivateLink avoids peering and works over ENIs, tends to be preferred by security teams.
[01:05] Ravi: When you say peering is simpler, do you mean latency is lower? Are there NAT/egress constraints?
[01:12] Jasper: Peering gives you an L3 route so yeah, lower hops, lower jitter, but you need route management and sometimes sharing subnets. PrivateLink routes via an endpoint in your VPC that sends to our service via AWS backbone, isolates your network more. Egress: both options can be configured so that no traffic leaves region; we can restrict endpoints to specific AZs/regions.
[01:36] Sofia: Our compliance req: data must not leave US physical boundaries. we also need to ensure that any logs that contain PHI are not stored outside the customer-controlled S3 / not sent to third parties. Do you support KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys?
[01:50] Jasper: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS for private deployments; for Hosted we offer BYOK options and HSM integrations for Private deployments. Audit logs are available and can be forwarded to your S3 or Splunk via secure forwarders.

[02:05] Elena: Workload specifics: we plan to run clinical summarization and chart extraction. Typical request is ~800 tokens output, inputs average 1.2k tokens. Peak concurrent sessions ~80 during batch ingest windows, baseline steady RPS ~12. We also plan embeddings for indexing — about 1M vectors initially, batched.
[02:27] Jasper: That’s helpful. For the summarization workload we’d recommend starting with our 8-GPU dedicated pool for the POC so we can measure throughput under realistic loads. For embeddings we’ll do parallel batch runs. For sizing benchmark: we’ll run 10k requests representative of your sample set with avg 800-token output to get p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[02:52] Ravi: Can you estimate costs for that POC run? and also what the expected p95 latencies might be?
[02:59] Maya: We’ll send a POC pricing sheet; rough POC cost for 4 weeks with reserved capacity is estimate in the doc but Jasper will produce a more concrete run cost after the benchmark. For latency, depends on model size and quantization; rough ballpark for our optimized variants: p50 ~300-600ms for short prompts, but for 800-token generations p95 could be in the multi-second range — typically 2–6s. Our goal is to get stable p95 under your success threshold.
[03:32] Sofia: For clinical use, acceptable p95 is 5s for summaries; anything higher is risky for end-user workflows. Also we need to know what data persists on your side (KV cache, logs).
[03:45] Jasper: Default runtime keeps ephemeral KV caches in memory per node and we persist only the minimal metrics unless you opt in. For Private deployment we can disable telemetry forwarding and keep logs in your VPC. KV cache is not written to disk by default.

[04:02] Elena: Success criteria we propose: (1) p95 latency for 800-token summaries <= 5s, (2) throughput able to handle 80 concurrent sessions with degradation <15% vs baseline, (3) no egress outside US, (4) audit logs and KMS with BYOK enabled. Are those things you can commit to for the POC?
[04:24] Maya: Yes we can run the POC to validate those. The POC acceptance will be benchmark-based: we’ll run tests with your sample dataset and measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cost per 1k tokens. If we meet the agreed thresholds, we close the POC successfully.
[04:40] Ravi: Networking detail: do you require us to open specific ports? How does authentication work for PrivateLink?
[04:48] Jasper: For PrivateLink we provide a service name you create an interface endpoint for; traffic goes over ENIs to our service, no public IP required. Authentication is via mTLS + short-lived tokens, and we can integrate with your SSO for provisioning. For peering you need route table entries to allow traffic to our IP ranges, and we’ll provide the IP blocks. No inbound ports open to the public.
[05:10] Sofia: If we do peering, our security team worries about route table sprawl and accidental lateral access. PrivateLink sounds cleaner but has some throughput tradeoffs?
[05:19] Jasper: PrivateLink has slightly higher per-request overhead but it’s typically negligible for our workloads. For very high throughput bursts peering can be slightly more efficient, but we can configure NLBs and scaling to handle it. For the POC — PrivateLink is often the faster compliance win.

[05:38] Elena: Regions: we want the service in us-east-1 primarily, us-west-2 for DR. Do you have infra in both regions?
[05:45] Maya: Yes, Redwood has capacity regions in us-east-1 and us-west-2. For the POC we can deploy in us-east-1 and optionally run DR tests in us-west-2. We’ll need your preferred subnet ranges and whether you want cross-region VPC peering or separate PrivateLink endpoints.

[06:02] Ravi: On egress constraints: we have a list of disallowed countries (EU no, APAC except specific partners). Can you guarantee traffic never leaves region?
[06:11] Jasper: We can restrict routing so that the path stays in-region and ensure that any 3rd-party telemetry is disabled. For model updates, if you opt for Redwood-managed model catalog, we’ll ensure images and weights are pulled from regional registries. We’ll include an explicit egress config in the networking guide.

[06:30] Maya: Benchmark plan and timeline — propose 4-week POC:
 Week 0 (days 1–3): Networking setup (PrivateLink or peering), KMS provisioning, provision POC cluster in us-east-1.
 Week 1: Baseline benchmark (10k requests from your sample data, 800-token avg), capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
 Week 2: Tuning — batch sizes, quantization profile, caching, autoscaling rules.
 Week 3: DR/region test and security validation (audit log delivery, KMS tests).
 Week 4: Final metrics review and POC acceptance.
[07:05] Elena: That timeline works for us as long as networking can be done in the first 48–72 hours.
[07:10] Ravi: We’ll need the exact PrivateLink service name and your IP ranges to create endpoint and route tables.
[07:16] Maya: I’ll send the service name and a step-by-step networking doc today. Jasper will run the baseline benchmark once the POC cluster is up — we prefer you run a small client within your VPC to simulate native traffic so we can measure end-to-end.

[07:30] Jasper: For benchmarks we’ll collect: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization, memory, and token cost. We’ll provide the benchmark spreadsheet with raw logs and a summary sheet. Expect a first pass report within 48 hours of running the 10k sample.
[07:48] Sofia: A couple security checks: do you retain request payloads by default? what about redaction?
[07:55] Jasper: By default hosted logs may keep traces for debugging but for Private we can disable payload retention and only keep anonymized metadata. We also offer on-prem options where nothing leaves the customer-controlled environment. We can enable automatic redaction for PII if you want.

[08:12] Elena: Success criteria recap: p95 <= 5s, handle 80 concurrent with <15% performance loss, BYOK/KMS, audit logs to our S3, no egress outside US. If benchmarks hit these we sign off.
[08:28] Maya: Sounds good. I’ll summarize and send an email with attachments: networking guide, SOC2 pack, POC pricing and the benchmark template.
[08:36] Ravi: One last: cost model — during POC do you expect us to purchase Reserved capacity or is there a trial?
[08:42] Maya: We can do a time-limited POC with a short reserved pool (monthly pro-rate) or trial credits for evaluation. I’ll include both options in the pricing doc.

[08:51] Sofia: ok thanks, please also include details on key rotation and KMS audit logs.
[08:57] Jasper: Noted, will include KMS integration steps, key rotation policy and examples for CloudTrail logs.

[09:05] Maya: Great — next steps / action items noted. Thanks everyone, we’ll follow up with docs and the timeline.
[09:12] Elena: Thanks all.

End recording.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had some label swaps (Speaker 2/3) and a few technical terms mis-transcribed (PrivateLink seen as “private link”, KV cache as “K V cash”) — verified by SE during call.
